newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh tribal insurgency seen nowhere near end.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh tribal insurgency seen nowhere near end.

text.p: Troops fighting separatist tribal insurgents in Bangladesh's Chittagong Hill Tracts say they see no prospects for ending the battle in the near future.
Civil servants say they feel nothing will be achieved in peace talks unless the rebels are forced to surrender arms, but soldiers say they are just tired.
"We are fed up," said Brigadier A.T.M. Zahirul Alam, counter-insurgency commander in Rangamati, one of three Hill Tract districts.
"Sometimes it comes too heavy on us," he told Reuters at his headquarters on Friday, adding that he himself has been assigned to combat areas in the Hill Tracts for a fifth time now.

The insurgency was begun by tribal Shanti Bahini (peace force), made up mostly of Chakma tribesmen, in the early 1970s over their demand for political autonomy, and intensified when the Bangladeshi government allowed Bengali-speaking Moslems to resettle in the Hill Tracts to ease overcrowding on the plains.
Thousands of Bengali families moved to the 5,500 square-mile (14,200 sq-km) Hill Tracts bordering India and Burma before the plan was suspended in 1985 in an effort to pacify insurgents.
The Shanti Bahini has never agreed to accept the outsiders and has had more than 20 rounds of peace talks with the government that produced no agreement.
Meanwhile, the government endorsed and continued extended a truce, which Hill Tracts officials said was unilaterally declared by the Shantis, in an endless search for peace.
But the rebels frequently violated the truce, and in the worst violation they killed 28 Bengali-speaking settlers in Rangamati district last month, officials said.

The current truce is due to expire on Thursday, while the government has reinforced its peace initiatives. It has set up a committee headed by Abul Hasnat Abdullah, Chief Whip of the ruling Awami League in parliament, to work out a peace formula.
Brigadier Alam was first assigned to the Hill Tracts in 1976 as a junior officer. His assignment started in March, 1996.
"I can see no change...no quick end to the insurgency. Rather I feel that we are back to square one."
Although the insurgency has often dwindled, it has regained its strength through new recruits and continuing support from outside the country, military and civil officials said.

The Shantis said they wanted a government response by Wednesday to pre-conditions they had set for a peace dialogue, proposed by the Parbatya Chattagram Janasanghati Samity (PCJSS), the political wing of the Shantis, Hill Tracts officials said.
"I guess nothing will be achieved...at least in the near future," one official said. He said the rebels were buying time to strengthen their rank and file, and possibly to procure arms.
The Hill Tracts -- comprising Rangamati, Khagrachhari and Bandarban districts -- now has a population of about one million, nearly 60 percent of them tribals.
Military sources said the Shantis, who claim to represent all the 13 tribes in the Hill Tracts, appeared to overstate their influence.

"Their main strength is the government's weakness," one source said. "And the main weakness of the government was that it had accepted an open-ended ceasefire unilaterally proposed by he insurgents," he said.

Under the ceasefire, security forces are prohibited from arresting rebels if they were not carrying arms. Besides, authorities have suspended elections to the Hill Tracts local councils indefinitely as asked by the rebels.
"We can see them...but cannot catch them. They move around, collect tolls and thus shake the confidence of ordinary people in the government," one official said.

According to official records, over 8,500 people have died in the 23-year insurgency, including 5,000 settlers, 3,000 tribals and sone 500 security forces. The exact number of rebel casualties were not known.
